```{r}
#| label: setup
library(targets)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggpubr)
library(lubridate)
```

This document will run the analysis for the manuscript

First, make sure everything is up to date:

```{r}
#| label: run targets pipeline
#| echo: true
tar_make()
```

### Population estimates

```{r}
density_cis <- tar_read("densities")

overall <- density_cis$`0.5`
overall_med <- round(median(overall), 1)
overall_low <- round(quantile(overall, 0.05), 1)
overall_high <- round(quantile(overall, 0.95), 1)
overall_text <- paste0(overall_med, " (", overall_low, "-", overall_high, ")")

by_year <- density_cis |>
	mutate(year = year(end_dates)) |>
	group_by(year) |>
	reframe(
		med_dens = round(median(`0.5`), 1),
		low_dens = round(quantile(`0.5`, 0.05), 1),
		high_dens = round(quantile(`0.5`, 0.95), 1)
	) |>
	mutate(text = paste0(med_dens, " (", low_dens, "-", high_dens, ")"))

text_2014 <- by_year |>
	filter(year == 2014) |>
	pull(text)

text_2025 <- by_year |>
	filter(year == 2025) |>
	pull(text)

model_data <- tar_read(model_data)
original_ids <- read_rds("../nfsdmp-predict/data/original_ids.rds")
df <- model_data |>
	filter(!propertyID %in% original_ids)

n_states <- length(unique(df$st_name))
n_year <- length(unique(year(df$end_dates)))
min_date <- min(df$start_dates)
max_date <- max(df$start_dates)
n_pp <- df |>
	select(propertyID, primary_period) |>
	distinct() |>
	nrow()
n_prop <- length(unique(df$propertyID))
```

Across the `r n_states` states and `r n_year` years where USDA-APHIS-WS removals occurred (n = `r n_pp` individual primary periods from `r min_date` to `r max_date` across `r n_prop` properties), the distribution of median posterior density estimates had a median of `r overall_text` wild pigs/km2. Note that these are not national scale density estimates, but rather a summary of estimated densities at properties where USDA-APHIS-WS conducted removals over this time period.

### Proportion of the population removed varies by method

```{r}
#| label: fig-removals
#| fig-cap: "Summary of the average proportion of the population removed by each method at each property. Boxplots represent the median and interquartile range (IQR), where the whiskers extend plus or minus 1.5 times the IQR."
tar_read(fig_prop_take)

df_actual <- tar_read("actual_percent_take")

n_by_state <- df_actual |>
	select(st_name, method) |>
	distinct() |>
	count(method)

n_state <- function(m) {
	n_by_state |>
		filter(method == m) |>
		pull(n)
}

n_fw <- n_state("Fixed wing")
n_gs <- n_state("Ground-shooting")
n_heli <- n_state("Helicopter")
n_snare <- n_state("Snare")
n_trap <- n_state("Trap")

n_by_prop <- df_actual |>
	select(propertyID, method) |>
	distinct() |>
	count(method)

p_prop <- function(m) {
	n <- n_by_prop |>
		filter(method == m) |>
		pull(n)
	round(n / n_prop * 100)
}

p_fw <- p_prop("Fixed wing")
p_gs <- p_prop("Ground-shooting")
p_heli <- p_prop("Helicopter")
p_snare <- p_prop("Snare")
p_trap <- p_prop("Trap")

by_state <- function(df) {
	df |>
		group_by(method, st_name) |>
		summarise(
			med = round(median(mu_prop_take), 2),
			low = round(quantile(mu_prop_take, 0.05), 2),
			high = round(quantile(mu_prop_take, 0.95), 2),
			n = n()
		) |>
		ungroup() |>
		filter(n > 1) |>
		mutate(text = paste0(med, " (", low, "-", high, ")"))
}

a_by_state <- by_state(df_actual)

a_trap <- a_by_state |> filter(method == "Trap")
n_trap_zero <- a_trap |> filter(med == 0) |> nrow()
max_trap <- a_trap |> filter(med == max(med))
trap_state <- max_trap$st_name
trap_text <- max_trap$text

a_snare <- a_by_state |> filter(method == "Snare")
n_snare_zero <- a_snare |> filter(med == 0) |> nrow()
max_snare <- a_snare |> filter(med == max(med))
snare_state <- max_snare$st_name
snare_text <- max_snare$text

a_gs <- a_by_state |> filter(method == "Ground-shooting")
min_ground <- a_gs |> filter(med == min(med))
if (nrow(min_ground) > 1) {
	min_ground <- min_ground |> filter(high == min(high))
}
min_ground_state <- min_ground$st_name
min_ground_text <- min_ground$text

max_ground <- a_gs |> filter(med == max(med))
max_ground_state <- max_ground$st_name
max_ground_text <- max_ground$text

a_fw <- a_by_state |> filter(method == "Fixed wing")
min_fw <- a_fw |> filter(med == min(med))
min_fw_state <- min_fw$st_name
min_fw_text <- min_fw$text

max_fw <- a_fw |> filter(med == max(med))
max_fw_state <- max_fw$st_name
max_fw_text <- max_fw$text

a_heli <- a_by_state |> filter(method == "Helicopter")
min_heli <- a_heli |> filter(med == min(med))
min_heli_state <- min_heli$st_name
min_heli_text <- min_heli$text

max_heli <- a_heli |> filter(med == max(med))
max_heli_state <- max_heli$st_name
max_heli_text <- max_heli$text
```

Traps represent the most frequently utilized method by USDA-APHIS-WS, being deployed by all states and on `r p_trap`% of properties (Table 1). There were `r n_trap_zero` states in which the median proportion of the population removed in a 4-week period by traps was zero, and the maximum came from `r trap_state` with a median of `r trap_text` (Figure 1). 
The second most utilized method was helicopters, which were deployed on `r p_heli`% of properties across `r n_heli` states. The median proportion of the population removed from helicopters ranged between the lowest in `r min_heli_state` at `r min_heli_text` and the highest in `r max_heli_state` at `r max_heli_text`.
Ground-shooting was the third most deployed method, being used on `r p_gs`% of properties across `r n_gs` states. The median proportion of the population removed from ground-shooting ranged between the lowest in `r min_ground_state` at `r min_ground_text` and the highest in `r max_ground_state` at `r max_ground_text`.
Snares represent the fourth most deployed method, being used on `r p_snare`% of properties across `r n_snare` states. For snares, there were `r n_snare_zero` states where the median proportion of the population removed was zero, and the maximum proportion removed came from `r snare_state` at `r snare_text`. 
Fixed-wing aircraft were used the least, on `r p_fw`% of properties across `r n_fw` states. These two states ranged between the lowest proportion of the population removed in `r min_fw_state` at `r min_fw_text` and the highest in `r max_fw_state` at `r max_fw_text`.

```{r}

by_metric <- function(df, m) {
	df |>
		group_by(method) |>
		summarise(
			med = round(median(.data[[m]]), 2),
			low = round(quantile(.data[[m]], 0.05), 2),
			high = round(quantile(.data[[m]], 0.95), 2),
			n = n()
		) |>
		ungroup() |>
		mutate(text = paste0(med, " (", low, "-", high, ")")) |> 
    select(method, text)
}

d1 <- df_actual |> by_metric("mu_prop_take") |> rename(APR = text)
d2 <- df_actual |> by_metric("property_area_km2") |> rename(Area = text)
d3 <- df_actual |> by_metric("total_effort_per") |> rename(Effort = text)
d4 <- df_actual |> distinct(propertyID, method) |> count(method)

left_join(d1, d2) |> 
  left_join(d3) |> 
  left_join(d4) |> 
  knitr::kable()

```

### Wild pig population growth rates vary in space

```{r}
#| label: fig-lambda
#| fig-cap: "Figure shows the average population growth rate at each property within each state. The number of properties (n) within each state are on the y-axis. A growth rate greater than one indicates that a property's population is growing. Values of zero represent properties that went extinct between the first and second observed primary periods. Boxplots represent the median and interquartile range (IQR), where the whiskers extend plus or minus 1.5 times the IQR."
tar_read(fig_lambda_hat_by_state)
```

```{r}
#| label: lambda analysis
df <- tar_read("mu_lambda") |>
	filter(!is.na(mu))

all_prop_med <- round(median(df$mu), 2)
all_prop_low <- round(quantile(df$mu, 0.05), 2)
all_prop_high <- round(quantile(df$mu, 0.95), 2)

n_props <- nrow(df)
n_declining <- df |>
	filter(mu < 1) |>
	nrow()
percent_declining <- round(n_declining / n_props * 100)

lambda_summary <- df |>
	group_by(st_name) |>
	summarise(
		n = n(),
		med = round(median(mu), 2),
		ymin = round(quantile(mu, 0.25), 2),
		ymax = round(quantile(mu, 0.75), 2),
	) |>
	arrange(med) |>
	mutate(text = paste0(med, " (", ymin, " - ", ymax, ")"))



low <- lambda_summary |>
	filter(n >= 10) |>
	filter(med == min(med))
state_low <- low$st_name
low_lambda <- low$text

high <- lambda_summary |>
	filter(med == max(med))
state_high <- high$st_name
high_lambda <- high$text

n_under_1 <- lambda_summary |>
	filter(med < 1) |>
	nrow()

n0 <- df |>
	filter(mu == 0) |>
	nrow()
```

Individual populations exhibited a range of average growth rates (Figure 2). Across all properties the median average population growth rate (lambda_hat) per 28-day period was `r all_prop_med` (`r all_prop_low`-`r all_prop_high`), meaning `r percent_declining`% (n = `r n_declining`) of properties had declining populations with ongoing control activities. There was also variation within and across states (Figure 2). For the states that had at least 10 properties, the lowest growth rate was `r state_low` where the median property had an average growth rate of `r low_lambda`, and the state with the highest growth rate was `r state_high` with a median of `r high_lambda`. There were `r n0` properties with a growth rate of zero, because they eradicated wild pigs between their first and second primary periods. Finaly, there were `r n_under_1` states where at least half of their properties had a declining population (Figure 2).

```{r}
# Appendix 1 Table S5
l_sum <- lambda_summary |>
	dplyr::rename(
		State = st_name,
		Distribution = text,
		`n properties` = n
	) |>
	arrange(State) |>
	select(State, Distribution, `n properties`) 
	
```



### Density is prevented due to management

```{r}
#| label: fig-trajectory
#| fig-cap: "The change in median wild pig density relative to the initial median density at year 0 over a five-year period. The boxplots represent the median and interquartile range (IQR) of these changes, where the whiskers extend plus or minus 1.5 times the IQR with outliers removed. The Without management scenario (orange) is the result of the bootstrapping procedure, and the With management scenario (purple) compares median posterior density estimates at the specified interval to the initial posterior density estimate at year zero. The facets represent the initial density category, where Low is less than 1 wild pig/km2, Medium is between 1-3 wild pigs/km2, High is between 3-5 wild pigs/km2, and Very high is greater than 5 wild pigs/km2."
tar_read(fig_epr)$density
```

```{r}
#| label: bootstap analysis
keep <- c(364, 728, 1092, 1456, 1820)
years_f <- sort(keep / 364)

df <- tar_read(bootstrap_mgmt) |>
	filter(delta_time %in% keep) |>
	mutate(years = delta_time / 364)

df_with <- df |>
	filter(
		mgmt == "With"
	) |>
	rename(
		density_with = density_estimate,
		delta_with = delta_density
	) |>
	select(-percent_change, -management, -mgmt)

df_without <- df |>
	filter(
		mgmt == "Without"
	) |>
	rename(
		density_without = density_estimate,
		delta_without = delta_density
	) |>
	select(-percent_change, -management, -mgmt)

cat_medians <- left_join(df_with, df_without) |>
	mutate(density_prevented = density_without - density_with) |>
	group_by(years, density_cat) |>
	summarise(
		med = round(median(density_prevented), 1),
		low = round(quantile(density_prevented, 0.05), 1),
		high = round(quantile(density_prevented, 0.95), 1),
		n = n()
	) |>
	ungroup() |>
	mutate(u = paste0(low, "-", high))

get_u <- function(df, dc, y, v) {
	df |>
		filter(
			density_cat == dc,
			years == y
		) |>
		pull(all_of(v)) |>
		unname()
}


vhigh_min <- df |>
	filter(
		mgmt == "With",
		density_cat == "Very high"
	) |>
	group_by(years) |>
	reframe(m = -1 * median(delta_density)) |>
	pull(m) |>
	min() |>
	round(2)

delta_density <- df |>
	group_by(density_cat, years, mgmt) |>
	summarise(
		med = round(median(delta_density), 1),
		low = round(quantile(delta_density, 0.05), 1),
		high = round(quantile(delta_density, 0.95), 1),
		n = n()
	) |>
	ungroup()

df |>
	group_by(density_cat, years, mgmt) |>
	reframe(q = median(delta_density))

q75 <- df |>
	filter(density_cat == "Low", years == 5) |>
	group_by(mgmt) |>
	summarise(q = quantile(delta_density, 0.75))

q75_w <- q75 |>
	filter(mgmt == "With") |>
	pull(q) |>
	round(2)
q75_wo <- q75 |>
	filter(mgmt == "Without") |>
	pull(q) |>
	round(2)

n_below_0 <- df |>
	filter(delta_density < 0, years == 5) |>
	group_by(mgmt, density_cat) |>
	summarise(n_below_0 = n())

n_all <- df |>
	filter(years == 5) |>
	group_by(mgmt, density_cat) |>
	summarise(n = n())

pfall <- left_join(n_all, n_below_0) |>
	mutate(
		n_below_0 = replace_na(n_below_0, 0),
		percent_fell = round(n_below_0 / n * 100, 1)
	)

get_p <- function(x, c) {
	pfall |>
		filter(
			density_cat == x,
			mgmt == c
		) |>
		pull(percent_fell)
}

p_w_l <- get_p("Low", "With")
p_wo_l <- get_p("Low", "Without")
p_w_m <- get_p("Medium", "With")
p_wo_m <- get_p("Medium", "Without")
p_w_h <- get_p("High", "With")
p_wo_h <- get_p("High", "Without")
p_w_vh <- get_p("Very high", "With")
p_wo_vh <- get_p("Very high", "Without")


low_1_med <- get_u(cat_medians, "Low", 1, "med")
low_1_low <- get_u(cat_medians, "Low", 1, "low") * -1
low_1_high <- get_u(cat_medians, "Low", 1, "high")
low_5_med <- get_u(cat_medians, "Low", 5, "med")
low_5_low <- get_u(cat_medians, "Low", 5, "low") * -1
low_5_high <- get_u(cat_medians, "Low", 5, "high")

cat_medians <- cat_medians |>
	mutate(t = paste0(med, " (", u, ")"))

med_1 <- get_u(cat_medians, "Medium", 1, "t")
high_1 <- get_u(cat_medians, "High", 1, "t")
vhigh_1 <- get_u(cat_medians, "Very high", 1, "t")

med_5 <- get_u(cat_medians, "Medium", 5, "t")
high_5 <- get_u(cat_medians, "High", 5, "t")
vhigh_5 <- get_u(cat_medians, "Very high", 5, "t")
```

The variation in the effect of management was more pronounced as the initial density increased and as more time elapsed (Figure 3). 
For example, the amount of density prevented (i.e. the difference between the simulations without management compared to what happened with management) when the initial density of wild pigs was low (i.e. <1 pigs/km2) increased only slightly over five years. 
For example, after one year there was a median of `r low_1_med` wild pigs/km2 prevented (90% CI of an increase of `r low_1_low` to a decrease of `r low_1_high` wild pigs/km2). 
This is compared to after five years of management, where we predicted a median of `r low_5_med` wild pigs/km2 prevented (90% CI of an increase of `r low_5_low` to a decrease of `r low_5_high` wild pigs/km2).
However, when management occurred, the most likely outcome after five years in the low-density scenario was to keep populations stable, which contrasted with the no management simulations in which populations were more likely to grow (Figure 3). 
Specifically, 75% of the low-density populations that experienced management grew by no more than `r q75_w` wild pigs/km2 while 25% of the simulations without management grew by at least `r q75_wo` wild pigs/km2 (Figure 3).

The amount of density prevented after one year increased with initial density, where `r med_1`, `r high_1`, and `r vhigh_1` wild pigs/km2 were prevented when initial density was medium (1-3 wild pigs/km2), high (3-5 wild pigs/km2), and very high (>5 wild pigs/km2), respectively (a negative density prevented indicates the population would increase by the specified amount; Figure 3). 
After five years, the amount of density prevented was `r med_5`, `r high_5`, and `r vhigh_5` wild pigs/km2, for the medium, high, and very high scenarios, respectively. 
The absolute drop in density with management was most apparent in the very high-density properties, where the median reduction in density across all years was at least `r vhigh_min` wild pigs/km2 (Figure 3).

Additionally, across all properties, wild pig densities fell after five years at `r p_w_l`%, `r p_w_m`%, `r p_w_h`%, and `r p_w_vh`% percent of properties in the low, medium, high, and very-high initial density scenarios, respectively. 
This contrasts with the simulations that did not conduct removals, where after five years wild pig densities fell at `r p_wo_l`%, `r p_wo_m`%, `r p_wo_h`%, and `r p_wo_vh`% percent of properties for the low, medium, high, and very high initial density scenarios, respectively.


### Population trajectories are modulated by effort and property size

```{r}
#| label: fig-epr
#| fig-cap: A) The average actual proportion of the population removed (APR) by each method in each property. B) The area of each property where methods where used. C) The average total effort per unit (TEPU) deployed for each method in each property. For A-C, the data are grouped into the EPT given the average growth rate of the property where the method was deployed. Events the led to population growth are in red, events that lead to a shrinking population are in light blue, and events that lead to a slashing population are in dark blue. D) The theoretical expected population trajectory (EPT) given a population's growth rate and APR. A value of -1 indicates eradication (blue), 0 indicates no change (white), and 1 indicates a populattion that is expected to double (red). The dotted line shows the threshold at which populations are expected to grow or increase, and the dashed line shows the threshold at which populations are expected to reduce by more (slash) or less (shrink) than half.
tar_read(fig_epr)

df <- tar_read(epr_data)

properties_m <- df |>
	group_by(method) |>
	count() |>
	ungroup()


make_epr_summaries <- function(df, y) {
	df |>
		group_by(method, epr_cat) |>
		summarise(
			med = as.character(round(median(.data[[y]]), 2)),
			low = round(quantile(.data[[y]], 0.05), 2),
			high = round(quantile(.data[[y]], 0.95), 2),
			n = n()
		) |>
		ungroup() |>
		left_join(properties_m) |>
		mutate(text = paste0(med, " (", low, "-", high, ")")) |>
		select(-med, -low, -high)
}


aprs <- make_epr_summaries(df, "mu_prop_take") |> rename(APR = text)
area <- make_epr_summaries(df, "property_area_km2") |> rename(Area = text)
effort <- make_epr_summaries(df, "effort_per_unit_per_area") |>
	rename(TEPUA = text)

epr_table <- left_join(aprs, area) |> left_join(effort)

get_mu <- function(df, y, v) {
	df |>
		group_by(epr_cat) |>
		summarise(
			mu = mean(.data[[y]])
		) |>
		ungroup() |>
		filter(epr_cat == v) |>
		pull(mu)
}

apr_grow <- df |> get_mu("mu_prop_take", "Increasing")
apr_shrink <- df |> get_mu("mu_prop_take", "Moderately declining")
apr_slash <- df |> get_mu("mu_prop_take", "Strongly declining")
apr_slash_shrink <- round(apr_slash / apr_shrink, 2)
apr_shrink_grow <- round(apr_shrink / apr_grow, 2)

area_grow <- df |> get_mu("property_area_km2", "Increasing")
area_shrink <- df |> get_mu("property_area_km2", "Moderately declining")
area_slash <- df |> get_mu("property_area_km2", "Strongly declining")
area_slash_grow <- round(area_grow - area_slash, 2)
area_shrink_grow <- round(area_grow - area_shrink, 2)

effort_grow <- df |> get_mu("effort_per_unit_per_area", "Grow")
effort_shrink <- df |> get_mu("effort_per_unit_per_area", "Shrink")
effort_slash <- df |> get_mu("effort_per_unit_per_area", "Slash")
effort_slash_shrink <- round(effort_shrink - effort_slash, 2)
effort_shrink_grow <- round(effort_grow - effort_shrink, 2)
```


Given the growth rate at the time of removals, we calculated that removals were most likely to have and EPT of moderately declining regardless of method used. 
For all methods, the second-most likely EPT was increasing, followed by strongly declining.

Across all methods, the APR needed to make a population strongly decline was, on average, greater than that required to make a population moderately decline by a factor of `r apr_slash_shrink`, and the APRs required to make a population moderately decline were greater than those that resulted in an increasing population by a factor of `r apr_shrink_grow`. 
For property area, across all methods, removal events that were expected to lead to an increase in population size were on properties `r area_shrink_grow` km2 larger than removal events conducted on properties expected to lead to a moderate decline, and on `r area_slash_grow` km2 larger than removal events conducted on properties expected to lead to a strongly decline.
Generalizing effort across methods was difficult because the unit of effort differs across methods (Table 1), and because each method is used in different ecological and management contexts (see Discussion). 
To attempt to generalize across methods (and therefore deployment context), we use a standardized metric of average total effort per unit deployed per area deployed (i.e. property area) to understand how the density of effort affects EPT. 
Here, the same pattern holds for all methods, where when the density of effort is greatest, removal events were expected to lead to a strong decline in the populstion, followed by a moderate decline, and the lowest effort density was expected to lead to population increase (Figure 4C).
